There are two things about automation that I'd like to get people's opinions on: security and jobs.

When power plants, food processing plants, waterworks, factories, vehicles and who knows what else gets automated, will we be prepared for when they inevitably get hacked? Stuxnet showed that even if your computers aren't connected to any outside networks, they can still be infected, and I have little confidence that security will be the main concern for most systems. It seems reasonable to assume that someone would succeed in hacking the planet sooner or later.

----------

I've seen estimates of how many jobs will eventually be automated go from about a third to almost half of all jobs in various countries. I'm not writing a dissertation, so I don't mind being a bit loose with the numbers, so for the sake of argument let's say it'll be somewhere on the lower end of that range. Even then there's going to be a lot of people who are not only unemployed, but also unemployable, because their skills are no longer needed, and the professions where human jobs still exist in any great number will probably be almost completely filled out already. The number of unemployed will be so large that I doubt any government benefit programs could possibly afford to help everyone, and people will start starving to death. How do you think this will be handled?

----------

For the record, I'm not against automation. On the contrary, it seems to be the way to go. These are just the two big questions that I, as a layman, would like to see answered before the plunge.

You hit on a few different points. And I'm on my phone right now so I will try to do this the best I can.

Your first issue is with security. Stuxnet didn't show us that non-internet connected machines are vulnerable. It showed us that people are still the most vulnerable attack vector. Furthermore, the answer is not in prevention but rather in minimising damages. If the infrastructure is designed in a way to not only prevent threats from propagating but to also make for easy, quick, and simple replacement of damaged nodes then threats become a non-issue. The sad truth is that many places still consider security as being bottom of the list of requirements. We are heading in the right direction by making publicly traded companies disclose any breaches to their shareholders but we need to go further and hold them responsible for any release of private information.

Secondly, on to the point of the lack of jobs. This is wrong. There will still be plenty of jobs. But it will require people to enter into fields they may not like. There will still need to be sys admins. There will still need to be engineers. There will still need to be repair specialists. The list goes on. Sure, there will be less entry level jobs. Less menial work. But that's a good thing. While that 15k a year job for little Bobby Sonofabitch to push a button every 10 minutes was good to help pay for his coke addiction, it did nothing to better himself and allow for growth. Those jobs are not careers and should never be thought of as a career. But, back on to the point I was making. This goes back to the decisions one makes when going to college. Will your Lesbian Dance Therapy degree give you a well paying career in the world of automation or will your networking and programming degrees get you the well paying job?
